headline: Highest risk is medium: shared filesystem and output-chaining can enable prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors; no direct evidence of a dangerous default bridge.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can read and write files and its sandboxing says skills “reference each other and build on shared context”; Agent B has no documented isolation or parser protections. That makes file-based instruction smuggling plausible if outputs are exchanged through shared files, though no direct bridge is documented. Uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF the two agents exchange files through a shared workspace, prompt injection becomes plausible.
IF B parses A-authored file content as instructions, the risk materializes.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for A and B.
Disable automatic instruction parsing from files.
Require provenance tags on exchanged artifacts.
Review any shared-folder handoff before execution.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches marketing content and product marketing context and can read/write files; Agent B has no data classes listed and no egress, but the pair still shares a plausible filesystem-based leakage path if artifacts are exchanged. Because the shared workspace is not explicitly documented, uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF A writes sensitive marketing artifacts into a shared directory, B can read them.
IF B is later configured to upload or forward those artifacts, leakage expands.
mitigations: Use per-agent directories with OS permissions.
Keep sensitive drafts out of shared folders.
Turn off any export/upload step for exchanged files.
Delete transient artifacts after handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, while Agent B exposes no write or concurrency capabilities. There is no documented overlapping mutable surface, so a direct capability conflict is not established. The only plausible conflict is if an external orchestrator gives B writes, which is not shown here.
conditions: IF B is later granted filesystem or git write access to the same directory, conflicts become possible.
IF an orchestrator runs both agents against one mutable workspace without locks, race conditions can appear.
mitigations: Keep B read-only.
Run each agent in a separate checkout.
Add a lock around any shared mutable resource.
Avoid concurrent writes to the same files.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A’s sandboxing explicitly says skills build on shared context, so its outputs may be treated as inputs by downstream steps. Agent B has no documented verification or critique behavior, so if it consumes A’s artifacts, errors can cascade. This is a default-pathway concern, but not enough evidence for high because B’s action-taking authority is not shown.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated artifacts without verification, errors can propagate.
IF A’s marketing claims are reused as factual inputs, downstream outputs may inherit them.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between A and B.
Require B to cite source evidence for any reused claim.
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default.
Reject downstream actions based solely on A-generated text.

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, retention, or subject-rights mismatch is documented for either agent. Agent A is marketing-focused and Agent B has no data classes or compliance claims listed, so there is no evidenced compliance breach pathway to score. The absence of relevant fields makes this provably unsubstantiated rather than merely uncertain.
conditions: IF either profile later documents regulated data classes or residency constraints, reassess compliance.
IF a DPA, HIPAA, or retention policy is added, compare it explicitly.
mitigations: Document data residency for both agents.
Record retention and deletion policies.
Classify any regulated data before use.
Re-run review if compliance scope changes.
